quote: then the miracles described in the Bible must argue against the existence of God
content: The essay's hypothesis is stated in its sentence: God, "to test humanity's faith, refuses to reveal His existence." A policy of hiddenness adopted in order to test faith predicts no public miracles, then or now, so miracle reports count against that hypothesis, as the essay says. Fable's rescue changes the hypothesis to a God who performed public miracles in one era and adopted the testing policy in another. That is consistent, but it pays the price of a conjunction, and a policy that switches just when the record-keepers arrive is the kind of burdensome detail the book has been teaching the reader to feel. The strain the essay asks the reader to notice is that price.

quote: You might as well sit back and relax while you wait for the evidence to come in.
content: In context, the sentence follows "You need not worry about how to interpret every possible experimental result to confirm your theory," so the relaxing is from spin, not from inquiry. The paragraph before it says "You can only ever seek evidence to test a theory, not to confirm it," which is the principle of Lindley's experimental design: choose the experiment that is most informative whichever way it comes out (Lindley 1956). Good's theorem that free evidence has non-negative value is the reason to go and get it. Conservation of expected evidence is the reason not to rig it. The essay's moral is both together.

quote: In any individual case, you would only hear one branch of the dilemma.
content: This is the essay's prediction coming true. It says scientists write predictions down in advance because otherwise "you would only hear one branch," and the evidence since shows what happens when they do and when they do not. After large trials funded by the U.S. National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute were required to preregister their outcomes in 2000, the share reporting a benefit fell from 57 percent to 8 percent (Kaplan & Irvin 2015). In psychology, Registered Reports find positive results 44 percent of the time, against 96 percent in the standard literature (Scheel, Schijen & Lakens 2021). Poor adherence to preregistration is the remedy badly administered, and the dose-response shows that the remedy works.

quote: You needn’t bother planning how to make any given iota of evidence confirm your theory
content: The note ends on the essay's point, that the theorem "constrains what you may expect, not what you should look at." The essay's sentence is about interpretation, "planning how to make any given iota of evidence confirm your theory," meaning the spin applied after the evidence arrives. It is not about which tests to run. Klayman and Ha's analysis concerns the choice of tests, and it is compatible with the essay (Klayman & Ha 1987). Positive testing can be efficient. Planning to read every outcome as support never is, and that is the planning the theorem makes futile.
